q: Amaravati is one of the following?
explanation: Amaravati is the seat of Amararama, one of the five Pancharamas built by Chalukya Bhima I; it is not a Shakti Peetha.

notes.text: - **Pancharamas built by:** **Chalukya Bhima I**, i.e. under the **Vengi (Eastern) Chalukyas** (APPSC PYQ ×2) – not Kubja Vishnuvardhana, Pulakesin II, Rajaraja Narendra, Kakatiyas or Vijayanagara.

q: Who built the Pancharamas in Andhra?

notes.text: - **Pancharamas built by:** **Chalukya Bhima I**, i.e. under the **Vengi (Eastern) Chalukyas** (APPSC PYQ ×2) – not Kubja Vishnuvardhana, Pulakesin II, Rajaraja Narendra, Kakatiyas or Vijayanagara.

q: During whose period were the Pancharamas built?
explanation: The Pancharamas were built under the Vengi (Eastern) Chalukyas by Chalukya Bhima I, long before the Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara.

notes.text: - **Pancharamas built by:** **Chalukya Bhima I**, i.e. under the **Vengi (Eastern) Chalukyas** (APPSC PYQ ×2) – not Kubja Vishnuvardhana, Pulakesin II, Rajaraja Narendra, Kakatiyas or Vijayanagara.

q:
To consolidate their authority, the Velanati chiefs forged marriage alliances with other mandalikas. Which of the following statement(s) about the marriage alliance of Velanati Chodas of Andhra Pradesh is/are correct?

A. Anama, the sister of Kondapadumati chief Buddharaja was given in marriage to the Haihaya chief of Palnadu.

- **Mailama (Mailamba)**, daughter of **Gonka II**, was married to the Palnadu Haihaya **Anugaraju**, who ruled Palnadu from **Gurajala** with Velanati support.

q: Which of the following is a South Indian dynasty that was known for its extensive maritime trade and connections with Southeast Asia?
explanation: The Cholas were the South Indian dynasty famed for maritime trade with South-East Asia (Srivijaya, Kadaram) and China. The Ahoms, Khasis and Jaintias are north-eastern.

notes.text: - **Maritime trade:** the Cholas = the South Indian dynasty of **maritime trade with South-East Asia** and China (APPSC ASO).

q: Which Chola princess was married to Rajaraja Narendra (1019-1061)?
explanation: Rajaraja Narendra married Ammanga Devi, daughter of Rajendra Chola I, on 16 August 1022. Kundavai, Rajaraja I's daughter, was married to his father Vimaladitya.

q:
Which of the following statements is / are incorrect?
I. Saktivarma had married Kundavai, the daughter of Raja Raja Chola I.
II. Raja Raja Narendra had married Ammangaidevi, the daughter of Rajendra Chola I.
III. Rajendra Chalukya had married Madurantaki, the daughter of Rajendra Chola II.
explanation: Only statement I is wrong: Rajaraja I married his daughter Kundavai to Vimaladitya, not Saktivarman. Rajaraja Narendra married Ammanga Devi (daughter of Rajendra I), and Rajendra Chalukya (Kulottunga I) married Madhurantaki, daughter of Rajendra II.

notes.text: - **Statements PYQ (G2):** "Saktivarma married Kundavai" ✗; the other two ✓ → **only I incorrect**.

q: Who was the first Chalukya-Chola king?
explanation: Kulottunga I (born Rajendra Chalukya, son of Rajaraja Narendra and Ammanga Devi) became Chola king in 1070 and was the first king of the Chalukya-Chola line. Vijayalaya, Rajendra I, Rajadhiraja and Rajaraja I were earlier pure Chola kings, and Rajaraja Narendra was an Eastern Chalukya.

notes.text: - **First Chalukya-Chola king:** **Kulottunga I** (G2 2011 ×2; G2 2012; APPSC PYQ) – not Rajaraja Narendra, Rajendra I, Rajadhiraja or Vijayalaya.

q: Identify the incorrect statement regarding the Cholas: B. C.
options: The Chola Empire was founded by Parantaka-I
key_text: The Chola Empire was founded by Parantaka-I
explanation: Vijayalaya, a Pallava feudatory at Uraiyur, founded the imperial Chola line by capturing Thanjavur in 850 CE, so 'founded by Parantaka I' is the incorrect statement. Parantaka I was Maduraikonda, Rajaraja I took the Maldives and Rajendra I built Gangaikondacholapuram.

notes.text: - **⚠ Trap:** "founded by **Parantaka I**" or "by Rajendra I" is false (APPSC G1 statement; APPSC 2023 Deputy).
- **Founder:** **Vijayalaya**, a **Pallava feudatory at Uraiyur**, captured **Thanjavur** from the **Muttaraiyars** in **850 CE** and founded the imperial line (9th century) (RAS 2016; APPSC G1).

q: Which of the following statement is CORRECT about Chola kings?
options: The Chola Empire was founded by Rajendra I.
Aditya I succeeded Vijayalaya to become the ruler of the empire.
Aditya I was popularly called the Victor of the Ganges.
key_text: Aditya I succeeded Vijayalaya to become the ruler of the empire.
explanation: Aditya I (871-907) succeeded his father Vijayalaya. Rajendra I did not found the empire, and the 'victor of the Ganges' (Gangaikonda) title belongs to Rajendra I, not Aditya I or Vijayalaya.

notes.text: - **Successor:** **Aditya I** (871–907) – defeated the last Pallava **Aparajita** and ended Pallava rule.

q: Who built Visakhapatnam city?
explanation: Kulottunga Chola I built Visakhapatnam, named Kulottunga Cholapatnam after himself. Arikesari II, Narasimha II and Pandurangadu are distractors.

notes.text: - **Visakhapatnam built by:** **Kulottunga Chola** (APPSC AP History PYQ) – not Arikesari II, Narasimha II or Pandurangadu.

q: Chidambaram, Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram were constructed by which rulers?
explanation: The temples at Chidambaram (enlarged), Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram are works of the Chola rulers; the Mauryas, Shakas and Kushanas had nothing to do with them.

notes.text: - **Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram:** all **Chola** works (APPSC).

q: Which of the following is the title of Rajendra Chola?
explanation: Gangaikonda Chola ('the Chola who took the Ganga') is Rajendra I's best-known title, taken after the Ganga expedition of 1022. Kadaram Kondan (option d) was also his title, so the question has two right options; Singalantaka and Telinga-kula-kala were titles of Rajaraja I.

notes.text: - **Rajendra I's titles (G2 2000):** Gangaikonda **and** Kadaram Kondan are both his; Singalantaka and Telinga-kula-kala belong to **Rajaraja I**.

q: In which battle did the Pallava Aparajitavarman defeat the Pandyas?
explanation: At Sripurambiyam (Thiruppurambiyam, c. 885) the Pallava Aparajita, with the Ganga Prithvipati I and the Chola Aditya I, defeated the Pandya Varaguna II. The victory mostly helped the Cholas, who soon overthrew Aparajita.

notes.text: - **Sripurambiyam:** the Pallava Aparajitavarman defeated the Pandyas there (APPSC G2 2000; APPSC PYQ) – not Peruvalanallur or Kanchipuram.

q: The 'Kadagam' under the Cholas was
explanation: Under the Cholas a Kadagam was an army cantonment (military camp). Off-topic Chola PYQ, moved.

q: In the Chola Kingdom, a very large village administered as a single unit was called:
explanation: A taniyur was a very large village (an important brahmadeya or nagaram) run as a separate unit, independent of the nadu. Kurram and nadu were groups of villages; a kottam was a group of nadus.

notes.text: - **Taniyur:** a **very large village** (an important brahmadeya or nagaram) **administered as a single, separate unit**, outside the nadu (APPSC G1) – not kurram, kottam or nadu.

q: Which was the central location of the trade centre in medieval Andhra?
explanation: Penugonda (West Godavari) was the central trade centre of medieval Andhra, where the Ayyavole and Manigramam guilds had 18 branches across Vengi.

notes.text: - **Penugonda** (West Godavari) = central trade centre of medieval Andhra (**APPSC G2 2012**); Ayyavole and Manigramam had **18 branches** across Vengi.

q: Preparation of the multi-armed Nataraja by the 'Cire Perdue' (lost-wax) technique is an ancient technology of whose time?
explanation: None of the options is the Cholas, under whom the lost-wax Nataraja was perfected. Of those given, the Pallavas are right: bronze images were already modelled and cast by cire perdue in the Pallava period (8th-9th c.), and the Chola bronzes grew out of that tradition.

notes.text: - **APPSC "cire perdue Nataraja" PYQ:** options lacked the Cholas; of those given, the **Pallavas** (earliest South Indian bronzes) is the defensible answer (Ikshvakus, Vishnukundins, Eastern Chalukyas did not make them).

- **Technique:** **lost-wax (cire perdue)** casting; bronze images were already cast in the **Pallava** period (8th–9th c.), but the **Chola** period (10th–12th c.) produced the finest; queen **Sembiyan Mahadevi** was a key patron.
